# Introduction
The goal for this project was to predict each player's K% from the 2025 season. We were
given data of pitchers with at least 1 batter faced from the 2021-2025 season. The given data 
contained only information about the pitchers total K%, total batters faced, age, and Stuff+. As allowed, I wanted to incorporate more statistical data for each pitcher, 
in which I was able to obtain from Baseball Savant (https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/),
and join it with the fangraphs data. Throughout this R Markdown file, I will explain my data, 
methodology, model ramifications, and analyze how my model performs on the 2025 players. 
This file contains only my own work, with the exception of a few coded plots, and is formatted to be completely reproducible. 

# Setup & Data

```{r load data, message = F, warning = F}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(lightgbm)
library(xgboost)

# stats.csv attached as a downloadable file
stats <- read.csv('~/Downloads/stats.csv')
data <- read.csv('~/Downloads/k_2026.csv')
```
## Data Description
For our model, I wanted to include pitcher statcast data such as `whiff%`, `called strikes`,
and pitch arsenal data including fastball/breaking/offspeed pitch usage, speed, spin, and etc. 
I was able to download that data from Baseball Savant, which included  48 custom pitcher stat 
columns of players with a minimum of 1IP from 2021-2025. Luckily both the Savant  and Fangraphs 
data used the same `Player ID` (which I verified), so I was able to join the data together,
which resulted in a total of 50 columns describing each pitchers stats from that season.

Pitcher metrics included `called_strikes`, `swinging_strikes`, `zone_swing&miss%`, `out-zone_swing%`, 
`whiff%`, `Stuff+`,  `fastball_usage`, `breaking_usage`, `offspeed_usage`, `fastball_avg_speed`, 
`breaking_avg_speed`, `offspeed_avg_speed`, `K%`, `TBF`, among others. Based on my intuition these
were metrics that could most impact a players next year strikeout rate. And the idea was that I could
use a players current season stats and difference in their stats from the previous season(s) to predict
their next season `K%`. 

## Data Engineering
When joining the data, I immediately ran into data quality issues. There were many NaN's, 
different column names, and missing data due to some players not having played in the previous 
season. The following shows my work in removing NaN's, renaming columns, and engineering a couple features.

```{r}
# Renaming data columns to match each other and provide better readability
data <- data %>%
  rename('K%' = 'K.',
         'Stuff+' = 'Stuff.') 
stats <- stats %>%
  rename('last_name, first_name' = 'last_name..first_name') %>% 
  select(-c('k_percent'))

# Identify NA's
data %>% 
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.))))
stats %>% 
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.))))
```

```{r}
# More data cleainging and adding feature `called_strike_and_whiff%`
stats <- stats %>%
  mutate(
    Name = str_replace_all(`last_name, first_name`, "([^,]+),\\s*(.+)", "\\2 \\1"),
    `CSW%` = (p_called_strike+p_swinging_strike)/p_total_pitches
  ) %>%
  drop_na(z_swing_miss_percent, oz_swing_miss_percent) %>% 
  select(-c('last_name, first_name'))

# Joining Savant with Fangraphs data
joined_data <- stats %>%
  left_join(data, by = c('year' = 'Season', 'player_id' = 'PlayerId')) %>%
  arrange(year, TBF)

# Filling in NaN's with 0's for pitch usage, and deselecting colinear/non-useful data
joined_data <- joined_data %>% 
  mutate(n_fastball_formatted = coalesce(n_fastball_formatted, 0),
         n_breaking_formatted = coalesce(n_breaking_formatted, 0),
         n_offspeed_formatted = coalesce(n_offspeed_formatted, 0)
         ) %>% 
  select(-c(player_age, p_formatted_ip, z_swing_percent, oz_swing_percent, out_zone_percent, in_zone_percent, fastball_avg_spin, fastball_avg_break_x, fastball_avg_break_z, fastball_avg_break, fastball_range_speed, breaking_avg_break_z, breaking_avg_break, breaking_range_speed, offspeed_avg_break_z, offspeed_avg_break, offspeed_range_speed, avg_best_speed, avg_hyper_speed, pitch_count_offspeed, pitch_count_fastball, pitch_count_breaking, p_total_pitches, p_total_strike, p_called_strike, p_swinging_strike, p_total_swinging_strike))
```

In order for us to include the lag (previous) season info for each player for a given year,
we need to separate the data into their seasons and then join the previous season(s) data then 
calculate the difference in features between the years. 

One feature that I also wanted to add was Tom Tango's Marcel projection tool (https://www.tangotiger.net/archives/stud0346.shtml). His 5/4/3 projection weighs recent season performance and pulls an estimate `K%` towards the league average. This is a baseline prediction for projecting `K%` based on historical data. Adding this as a feature gives our model a bayesian prior that prevents the model from overweighting a lucky pitcher that had a good season. 

```{r}
#Separating data by year, adding a year suffix on the end of each feature
joined_data_2021 = joined_data %>% filter(year == 2021)
joined_data_2021 <- joined_data_2021 %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0(., "_21"), .cols = -c(player_id, year, Name.x, Name.y, Team))

joined_data_2022 = joined_data %>% filter(year == 2022)
joined_data_2022 <- joined_data_2022 %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0(., "_22"), .cols = -c(player_id, year, Name.x, Name.y, Team))

joined_data_2023 = joined_data %>% filter(year == 2023)
joined_data_2023 <- joined_data_2023 %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0(., "_23"), .cols = -c(player_id, year, Name.x, Name.y, Team))

joined_data_2024 = joined_data %>% filter(year == 2024)
joined_data_2024 <- joined_data_2024 %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0(., "_24"), .cols = -c(player_id, year, Name.x, Name.y, Team))

joined_data_2025 = joined_data %>% filter(year == 2025)
joined_data_2025 <- joined_data_2025 %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0(., "_25"), .cols = -c(player_id, year, Name.x, Name.y, Team))

# Joining 2022 & 2021 pitcher stats onto 2023 pitchers
stack_2023 <- joined_data_2023 %>% 
  left_join(
    joined_data_2022 %>% select(-c(Name.x, Name.y, Team, year)), 
    by = c('player_id')
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    joined_data_2021 %>% select(-c(Name.x, Name.y, Team, year)), 
    by = c('player_id')
  )

# Getting feature columns from 2022 and 2021
base_cols <- colnames(joined_data_2022 %>% select(-c('player_id', 'year', 'Name.x', 'Name.y', 'Team', 'Age_22')))
prev_cols <- str_replace(base_cols, "_22$", "_21")
diff_cols <- str_replace(base_cols, "_22$", "_diff")

# Calculating the difference for each feature between 2022 and 2021
stack_2023[diff_cols] <- stack_2023[base_cols] - stack_2023[prev_cols]

# Marcels projection of K% for 2023 season
stack_2023 <- stack_2023 %>% 
  mutate(
    total_so = `K%_22` * TBF_22,
    Age_22 = coalesce(Age_22, Age_23 - 1),
    age_adj = if_else(Age_22 > 29, Age_22 * 0.006, Age_22 * 0.003)
  )
league_K <- sum(stack_2023$total_so, na.rm = TRUE) /
              sum(stack_2023$TBF_22, na.rm = TRUE)
stack_2023 <- stack_2023 %>% 
  mutate(
    num = 5 * coalesce(`K%_22`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_22, 0) + 
          4 * coalesce(`K%_21`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_21, 0) + 
          0 + 
          500 * league_K,
    den = 5 * coalesce(TBF_23, 0) + 
          4 * coalesce(TBF_22, 0) + 
          0 + 
          500,
    marcels_22 = num / den * age_adj
  )

# Selecting only stats from previous season and the difference since the last season before that.
# Also adding a binary variable to signify new pitchers, as well as updating `Age` variable.
stack_2023 <- stack_2023 %>% 
  mutate(is_new_22 = if_else(is.na(`K%_22`), 1, 0)) %>% 
  select(ends_with("_22"), ends_with("_diff"), `K%_23`, TBF_23) %>%
  rename_with(~ str_remove(., "_23$")) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("prev_", str_remove(., "_22$")), ends_with("_22"))

# Joining 2023 & 2022 pitcher stats onto 2024 pitchers 
stack_2024 <- joined_data_2024 %>% 
  left_join(
    joined_data_2023 %>% select(-c(Name.x, Name.y, Team, year)), 
    by = c('player_id')
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    joined_data_2022 %>% select(-c(Name.x, Name.y, Team, year)), 
    by = c('player_id')
  ) %>% 
  left_join(
    joined_data_2021 %>% select(player_id, `K%_21`, TBF_21),
    by = c('player_id')
  )
# Getting feature columns from 2022 and 2021
base_cols <- colnames(joined_data_2023 %>% select(-c('player_id', 'year', 'Name.x', 'Name.y', 'Team', 'Age_23')))
prev_cols <- str_replace(base_cols, "_23$", "_22")
diff_cols <- str_replace(base_cols, "_23$", "_diff")

# Calculating the difference for each feature between 2022 and 2021
stack_2024[diff_cols] <- stack_2024[base_cols] - stack_2024[prev_cols]

# Marcels projection of K% for 2024 season
stack_2024 <- stack_2024 %>% 
  mutate(
    total_so = `K%_23` * TBF_23,
    Age_23 = coalesce(Age_23, Age_24 - 1),
    age_adj = if_else(Age_23 > 29, Age_23 * 0.006, Age_23 * 0.003)
  )
league_K <- sum(stack_2024$total_so, na.rm = TRUE) /
              sum(stack_2024$TBF_23, na.rm = TRUE)
stack_2024 <- stack_2024 %>% 
  mutate(
    num = 5 * coalesce(`K%_23`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_23, 0) + 
          4 * coalesce(`K%_22`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_22, 0) + 
          3 * coalesce(`K%_21`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_21, 0) + 
          500 * league_K,
    den = 5 * coalesce(TBF_23, 0) + 
          4 * coalesce(TBF_22, 0) + 
          3 * coalesce(TBF_21, 0) + 
          500,
    marcels_23 = num / den * age_adj
  )

# Selecting only stats from previous season and the difference since the last season before that.
# Also adding a binary variable to signify new pitchers, as well as updating `Age` variable.
stack_2024 <- stack_2024 %>% 
  mutate(is_new_23 = if_else(is.na(`K%_23`), 1, 0)) %>% 
  select(ends_with("_23"), ends_with("_diff"), `K%_24`, TBF_24) %>%
  rename_with(~ str_remove(., "_24$")) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("prev_", str_remove(., "_23$")), ends_with("_23"))

# Stacking two dataframes to create training data
train_data <- bind_rows(stack_2024, stack_2023)
```

# Methodology

## Data Constraints
As previously explained, the idea was to use a players previous season stats and difference in stats 
from the year before that to predict the current season `K%`. There were some problems that immediately came 
to my mind at first.

(1) Positional Pitchers.

Some of these pitchers in our data are not pitchers, and are positional pitchers that pitched because
they were in a blowout. Without further data description it was hard to identify and filter out
the positional pitchers since even though they pitched in very little games, there were also real pitchers
that pitched a little amount of games that either got injured or just didn't pitch a whole lot. I didn't
want to filter out all pitchers that didn't pitch to say more than 50 batters for the sake of the real 
pitchers that also pitched to a less amount of batters. For example Seranthony Dominguez pitched to only 
3 batters in 2021 and then pitched to 207 the next year, while maintaining a similar K% and Stuff+ for 
both years. I didn't want to lose the information that 2021 Seranthony could carry for the model. So I
just left that data in there since it's unlikely there a huge sample of positional pitchers.

(2) Pitchers with Small TBF.

Clearly not every pitcher pitches to the same amount of batters every year. Relief pitchers pitch to 
a much smaller sample size of batters and are usually in more high stakes situations. Although our 
strikeout metric is already standardized, pitchers that faced less batters may have 
an inflated strikeout rate since they don't pitch to as many batters. So to deal with that, I decided to use `total_batters_faced` as weights for each pitcher, where our model will weigh down those pitchers with
inflated strikeout rates. In my implementation, the weights are set as $sqrt(TBF)$, which will prevent low
sample pitchers with inflated/random `K%` from skewing our data. This also assists with the positional pitcher issue. To note, we do have the marcels metric as a feature as a projection already but even that isn't perfect so this will assist on top of that.

(3) Pitchers with incomplete arsenals.

For pitchers that don't have a fastball/breaking/offspeed pitch in their arsenal, the data
by default leaves it as NaN, which we don't want. By coalescing the usage to 0% instead of having NaN, 
it allows us to place those pitchers with other pitchers who don't use that pitch on a similar level.

# Model Training
I had two different model types to test. A linear model and tree-based model. I trained a GLM model
at first on the data as a baseline model. A GLM model can capture the non-linear relationship between variables. However I wanted totrain an LightGBM and XGBoost model, as a tree based model is better for dealing with non-linear relationships, handles outliers well, and handles missing data that we want to keep. 

### GLM Model
```{r}
set.seed(8)

glm_train <- train_data
# 80/20 train test split
train_indices <- sample(1:nrow(glm_train), size = 0.8 * nrow(glm_train))
train_df <- glm_train[train_indices, ]
test_df  <- glm_train[-train_indices, ]

# Model training using GLM
base_model <- glm(`K%` ~ ., data = train_df, family = quasibinomial(link = "logit"))

# Predict on test data
test_df$predicted_so <- predict(base_model, newdata = test_df, type = "response")

# Find difference in error between pred and actual
errors <- test_df$`K%` - test_df$predicted_so

print(paste("MSE:", 
            sprintf("%.4f", sqrt(mean(errors^2, na.rm=TRUE)))))
print(paste("R^2:", 
            sprintf("%.4f", cor(test_df$predicted_so, test_df$`K%`, use = "complete.obs")^2)))
```
```{r}
ggplot(test_df, aes(x = `predicted_so`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

We can see that our base model has a MSE of 0.055 and R^2 of 28%, where our model explains ~28% of variance in our data. However our model does not work for instances with NaN's and we cannot replace all NaN's or drop those rows of data. So we cannot use this model. 

### LGB Model
```{r, results='hide'}
set.seed(9)

# 80/20 train test split
train_indices <- sample(1:nrow(train_data), size = 0.8 * nrow(train_data))
train_df <- train_data[train_indices, ]
test_df  <- train_data[-train_indices, ]
feature_cols <- setdiff(names(train_data), c('K%', 'TBF'))

X_train <- as.matrix(train_df[, feature_cols])
y_train <- train_df$`K%`
w_train <- sqrt(train_df$TBF)

X_test  <- as.matrix(test_df[, feature_cols])
y_test  <- test_df$`K%`
w_test  <- sqrt(test_df$TBF)

dtrain <- lgb.Dataset(data = X_train, label = y_train, weight = w_train)
dtest  <- lgb.Dataset(data = X_test,  label = y_test,  weight = w_test, reference = dtrain)

# Initialize parameters
params <- list(
  objective          = "regression",
  metric             = "rmse",
  learning_rate      = 0.01,
  num_leaves         = 7,
  min_data_in_leaf   = 40,
  feature_fraction   = 0.65,  
  bagging_fraction   = 0.80,   
  bagging_freq       = 1,
  lambda_l1          = 0.5, 
  lambda_l2          = 1.0   
)

valids <- list(train = dtrain, test = dtest) 

# Train LGB model
model_lgb <- lgb.train(
  params                = params,
  data                  = dtrain,
  nrounds               = 1000,
  valids                = valids,
  early_stopping_rounds = 50,
  verbose               = 1
)

# Predict on test set
test_df$`pred_K%` <- predict(model_lgb, X_test)

print(summary(test_df$`pred_K%`))

rmse_val <- sqrt(mean((test_df$`K%` - test_df$`pred_K%`)^2))
r2_val   <- cor(test_df$`K%`, test_df$`pred_K%`)^2

print(paste0("Test RMSE: ", sprintf("%.4f", rmse_val)))
print(paste0("Test R²:   ", sprintf("%.4f", r2_val)))

# Feature Importance
importance <- lgb.importance(model_lgb, percentage = TRUE)
lgb.plot.importance(importance, top_n = 20, measure = "Gain")

ggplot(test_df, aes(x = `pred_K%`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(prev_is_new)), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "orange"),
    labels = c("0" = "Existing", "1" = "New"),
    name = "Player Status"
  ) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

In this model, our test results give us a RMSE of 0.06 and R^2 of 22%. From our feature importance plot we can see that last seasons strikeout rate, zone swing & miss%, whiff%, fastball avg speed, and stuff+ are our best predictors. However when looking at our plot of actual vs predicted `K%`, we can see that we have a handful of new pitchers that are skewing our predictions. Which makes sense because without previous season data our model just makes normal random guesses for new pitchers, which seem to average out at ~22.5%. So if we take away those new pitchers, we can see how our model does on existing pitchers.

```{r}
# removing new pitchers
no_rooks <- test_df %>% filter(!is.na(prev_TBF))

# Test RMSE and R^2
print(paste0("Test RMSE: ", sprintf("%.4f", sqrt(mean((no_rooks$`K%` - no_rooks$`pred_K%`)^2)))))
print(paste0("Test R²: ", sprintf("%.4f", cor(no_rooks$`K%`, no_rooks$`pred_K%`, use = "complete.obs")^2)))

ggplot(no_rooks, aes(x = `pred_K%`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Now we get an improved RSME of 0.0566 and R^2 of 29%. 

### XGBoost Model
```{r, results='hide'}
X_train <- as.matrix(train_df[, feature_cols])
y_train <- train_df$`K%`
w_train <- sqrt(train_df$TBF)

X_test  <- as.matrix(test_df[, feature_cols])
y_test  <- test_df$`K%`
w_test  <- sqrt(test_df$TBF)

dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = X_train, label = y_train, weight = w_train)
dtest  <- xgb.DMatrix(data = X_test,  label = y_test,  weight = w_test)

params <- list(
  objective        = "reg:squarederror", # Robust to extreme fluke reliever seasons
  eval_metric      = "rmse",
  eta              = 0.02,                   # Low learning rate for stable convergence
  max_depth        = 3,                      # Shallow depth prevents fitting single-season noise
  min_child_weight = 10,                     # Enforces large sample support per leaf
  subsample        = 0.75,                   # Row subsampling
  colsample_bytree = 0.75,                   # Feature subsampling
  lambda           = 5.0,                    # L2 regularization (Ridge penalty)
  alpha            = 0.5                     # L1 regularization (Lasso penalty)
)

watchlist <- list(train = dtrain, test = dtest)

model_xgb <- xgb.train(
  params                = params,
  data                  = dtrain,
  nrounds               = 1000,
  watchlist             = watchlist,
  early_stopping_rounds = 40,
  print_every_n         = 20
)

test_df$`pred_K%` <- predict(model_xgb, dtest)

rmse_all <- sqrt(mean((test_df$`K%` - test_df$`pred_K`)^2))
r2_all   <- cor(test_df$`K%`, test_df$`pred_K`)^2

print(paste0("Test RMSE: ", sprintf("%.4f", rmse_all)))
print(paste0("Test R²:   ", sprintf("%.4f", r2_all)))

importance_matrix <- xgb.importance(feature_names = feature_cols, model = model_xgb)
xgb.plot.importance(importance_matrix = importance_matrix, top_n = 20)

ggplot(test_df, aes(x = `pred_K%`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(prev_is_new)), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "orange"),
    labels = c("0" = "Existing", "1" = "New"),
    name = "Player Status"
  ) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

For our XGBoost model, our test results give us a RMSE of 0.06 and R^2 of 22%. From our feature importance plot we can see that last seasons strikeout rate, zone swing & miss%, whiff%, stuff+, and fastball avg break/speed are our best predictors. However we see the similar issue of new pitchers that skew our predictions. We can similarly take away those new pitchers and see how our model does on existing pitchers.

```{r}
# removing new pitchers
no_rooks <- test_df %>% filter(!is.na(prev_TBF))

# Test RSME and R^2
print(paste0("Test RMSE: ", sprintf("%.4f", sqrt(mean((no_rooks$`K%` - no_rooks$`pred_K%`)^2)))))
print(paste0("Test R²: ", sprintf("%.4f", cor(no_rooks$`K%`, no_rooks$`pred_K%`, use = "complete.obs")^2)))

ggplot(no_rooks, aes(x = `pred_K%`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Now we get an RSME of 0.0571 and R^2 of 29%. 

XGBoost slightly outperforms LightGBM so we will use the XGB model. 

# Analysis
## Testing on 2025 data
Using the same setup and feature selection, we can test our model on 2025 data. 

```{r}
# Joining 2024 & 2023 pitcher stats onto 2025 pitchers
test_2025 <- joined_data_2025 %>% 
  left_join(
    joined_data_2024 %>% select(-c(Name.x, Name.y, Team, year)), 
    by = c('player_id')
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    joined_data_2023 %>% select(-c(Name.x, Name.y, Team, year)), 
    by = c('player_id')
  ) %>% 
  left_join(
    joined_data_2022 %>% select(player_id, `K%_22`, TBF_22),
    by = c('player_id')
  )

# Getting feature columns from 2024 and 2023
base_cols <- colnames(joined_data_2024 %>% select(-c('player_id', 'year', 'Name.x', 'Name.y', 'Team', 'Age_24')))
prev_cols <- str_replace(base_cols, "_24$", "_23")
diff_cols <- str_replace(base_cols, "_24$", "_diff")


# Calculating the difference for each feature between 2022 and 2021
test_2025[diff_cols] <- test_2025[base_cols] - test_2025[prev_cols]

# Marcels projection of K% for 2025 season
test_2025 <- test_2025 %>% 
  mutate(
    total_so = `K%_24` * TBF_24,
    Age_24 = coalesce(Age_24, Age_25 - 1),
    age_adj = if_else(Age_24 > 29, Age_24 * 0.006, Age_24 * 0.003)
  )
league_K <- sum(test_2025$total_so, na.rm = TRUE) /
              sum(test_2025$TBF_24, na.rm = TRUE)
test_2025 <- test_2025 %>% 
  mutate(
    num = 5 * coalesce(`K%_24`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_24, 0) + 
          4 * coalesce(`K%_23`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_23, 0) + 
          3 * coalesce(`K%_22`, 0) * coalesce(TBF_22, 0) + 
          500 * league_K,
    den = 5 * coalesce(TBF_24, 0) + 
          4 * coalesce(TBF_23, 0) + 
          3 * coalesce(TBF_22, 0) + 
          500,
    marcels_24 = num / den * age_adj
  )

# Selecting only stats from previous season and the difference since the last season before that.
# Also adding a binary variable to signify new pitchers, as well as updating `Age` variable.
test_2025 <- test_2025 %>% 
  mutate(is_new_24 = if_else(is.na(`K%_24`), 1, 0)) %>% 
  select(player_id, year, Name = Name.x, Team, Age_25, `Stuff+_25`, ends_with("_24"), ends_with("_diff"), `K%_25`, TBF_25) %>%
  rename_with(~ str_remove(., "_25$")) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("prev_", str_remove(., "_24$")), ends_with("_24"))

# Initialize Test Dataset
feature_cols <- setdiff(names(test_2025), c('player_id', 'year', 'Name', 'Team', 'Age', 'K%', 'TBF', 'Stuff+'))
X_test  <- as.matrix(test_2025[, feature_cols])

# Predict on test dataset using LGB model
test_2025$`pred_K%` <- predict(model_xgb, X_test)

# Test RSME and R^2
rmse_val <- sqrt(mean((test_2025$`K%` - test_2025$`pred_K%`)^2))
r2_val   <- cor(test_2025$`K%`, test_2025$`pred_K%`)^2

print(paste0("Test RMSE: ", sprintf("%.4f", rmse_val)))
print(paste0("Test R²:   ", sprintf("%.4f", r2_val)))

ggplot(test_2025, aes(x = `pred_K%`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(prev_is_new)), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "orange"),
    labels = c("0" = "Existing", "1" = "New"),
    name = "Player Status"
  ) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Our model gives us a RMSE of 0.06 and R^2 of 18% on our 2025 test data. 

```{r}
# removing new pitchers
no_rooks <- test_2025 %>% filter(prev_is_new == 0)

# Test RSME and R^2
print(paste0("Test RMSE: ", sprintf("%.4f", sqrt(mean((no_rooks$`K%` - no_rooks$`pred_K%`)^2)))))
print(paste0("Test R²: ", sprintf("%.4f", cor(no_rooks$`K%`, no_rooks$`pred_K%`, use = "complete.obs")^2)))

ggplot(no_rooks, aes(x = `pred_K%`, y = `K%`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted K%",
    x = "Predicted K%",
    y = "Actual K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

On existing pitchers, our model has an RSME of 0.05 and R^2 of 27% on existing pitchers.

```{r}
test_2025 <- test_2025 %>% 
  mutate(pred_diff = `pred_K%` - `K%`) %>% 
  select(player_id, year, Name, Team, TBF, `Stuff+`, Age, `K%`, `pred_K%`, pred_diff, prev_is_new) %>% 
  arrange(desc(`pred_K%`))
```

## Results
These are the top 5 projected pitchers by strikeout rate for 2025 that our model predicts:

```{r}
test_2025 %>% arrange(desc(`pred_K%`)) %>% slice(1:5)
```

These are the bottom 5 projected pitchers by strikeout rate for 2025 that our model predicts:

```{r}
test_2025 %>% arrange(`pred_K%`) %>% slice(1:5)
```

These are the top 5 closest predictions our model makes to the actual strikeout rate:

```{r}
test_2025 %>% slice_min(abs(pred_diff), n = 5)
```

These are the top 5 furthest predictions our model makes to the actual strikeout rate:

```{r}
test_2025 %>% slice_max(abs(pred_diff), n = 5)
```

If you notice for rows with a higher difference in prediction vs actual, we can see the TBF values are low. Meanwhile for the ones with low difference in pred vs actual, the TBF are mostly high. We can look at the trend in TBF values against the difference in prediction rates for `K%`:

```{r}
TBF_trend <- test_2025 %>%
  arrange(pred_diff)

ggplot(TBF_trend, aes(x = pred_diff, y = TBF)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#2E86AB", size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#E9724C", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "TBF Trend vs Prediction Difference",
    x = "Prediction Difference",
    y = "TBF"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

This plot validates our suspicion. The lower the TBF, the higher the difference is in our prediction. So lets take a closer look at the 'non-rookies' (just players who weren't in the league previously). Using LLM's assistance we are able to code a plot to view our overall results and how our model performs on each pitcher. X-axis is the difference between predicted and actual `K%` so the closer to 0 the better. And the Y-axis is the predicted `K%`. 

```{r}
# Filter to only non-new players
no_rooks <- test_2025 %>% filter(prev_is_new == 0)

# Get select players to label on plot for each quadrant
label_points <- bind_rows(
  # Top left (Under-predicted best pitchers)
  no_rooks %>%
    filter(pred_diff < 0, `pred_K%` > 0.225) %>%
    slice_max(`pred_K%`, n = 3),
  
  # Top right (Over-predicted best pitchers)
  no_rooks %>%
    filter(pred_diff > 0, `pred_K%` > 0.225) %>%
    slice_max(`pred_K%`, n = 3),
  
  # Bottom left (Under-predicted worst pitchers)
  no_rooks %>%
    filter(pred_diff < 0, `pred_K%` < 0.225) %>%
    slice_min(pred_diff, n = 3),
  
  # Bottom right (Over-predicted worst pitchers)
  no_rooks %>%
    filter(pred_diff > 0, `pred_K%` < 0.2) %>%
    slice_max(pred_diff, n = 3),
  
  # Midde (Accurately predicted)
  no_rooks %>%
    slice_min(abs(pred_diff), n = 3)
)

# Create visual
ggplot(no_rooks, aes(x = pred_diff, y = `pred_K%`)) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.225,
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#2E86AB") +
  
  # Labels for selected points
  geom_text_repel(
    data = label_points,
    aes(label = Name),
    size = 3,
    box.padding = 0.5,
    point.padding = 0.3,
    max.overlaps = Inf
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.05,
    y = min(no_rooks$`pred_K%`, na.rm = TRUE) - 0.02,
    label = "Over-predict",
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = -0.05,
    y = min(no_rooks$`pred_K%`, na.rm = TRUE) - 0.02,
    label = "Under-predict",
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(no_rooks$pred_diff, na.rm = TRUE),
    y = 0.225,
    label = "League Avg",
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Non-New Pitcher Predictions",
    x = "Prediction Difference",
    y = "Predicted K%"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

We can see the model slightly under-predicts high K-rate players like Mason Miller and Josh Hader, while is accurate for pitchers like Mason Montgomery and Tyler Alexander. The model under-predicts pitchers like Lucas Gilbreath and Ty Adcock, while over-predicts for low usage pitchers like Joe La Sorsa and Randy Dobnak. However for those pitcher I just mentioned, they have a low sample of batters faced, so it makes sense our model will over/under predict on those pitchers.

```{r}
pct_over <- mean(no_rooks$pred_diff > 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
pct_under <- mean(no_rooks$pred_diff < -0.05, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
pct_close <- mean(abs(no_rooks$pred_diff) <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) * 100

print(paste0("Over-predicts: ", round(pct_over, 1), "%"))
print(paste0("Under-predicts: ", round(pct_under, 1), "%"))
print(paste0("Close/accurate (within ±0.05): ", round(pct_close, 1), "%"))
```

## Discussion
So overall our model underperforms. Our model explains ~20% of 2025's pitcher variance, and is 43.7% correlated to the actual `K%`. Pitchers with fluke seasons and not enough samples get weighted too much. For non-new pitchers our model actually seems to perform decent, however on new or low usage pitchers the model has trouble with. Navigating those roadblocks have been difficult and the model is not as solid as I would have like it to have performed That said, I believe the model doesn't necessarily fail, as it still closely predicts ~70% of non-new pitchers within a 5% threshold of the true `K%` for the 2025 season. I believe with more work and more data, the model can improve to become a standard predictor of strikeout rates for seasons to come. 

Future considerations include a separate model for rookies, refining features, in-depth hyperparameter tuning, and adding more historical data as well as additional features that could play a role in prediciting strikeout rates.
